chunk-001:c001.proposition: Paul's early undisputed letters attest that he believed Christ underwent bodily resurrection and that Paul experienced an appearance of the risen Christ.

orphanFallback.rationale: The excerpt affirmatively presents the early Pauline corpus as evidence of bodily-resurrection belief and Paul's claimed encounter, so the proposition stands without an opposing antecedent.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: The contrast between mortal and spiritual bodies in 1 Corinthians 15 is best understood as describing a tangible, real, physical resurrected body rather than an immaterial body.

orphanFallback.rationale: Even without an earlier opposing move, Albrecht's lexical reading of the mortal-body and spiritual-body contrast independently supports a physical interpretation of Paul's resurrection claim.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: Unlike the acknowledged interpolation in Josephus, the extensive New Testament and Septuagint manuscript traditions generally do not exhibit comparable meaning-breaking textual alterations.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source comparison between Josephus and the manuscript traditions supplies an affirmative argument for substantive textual stability even if no prior corruption objection is retained.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Early Pauline material and hostile pagan descriptions identify a historically rooted Christian group whose beliefs about the crucified and worshiped Christ correspond to scriptural rather than Gnostic markers.

orphanFallback.rationale: The cited Pauline and hostile-pagan evidence can independently identify the beliefs of an early Christian group, so the same proposition remains constructive without a retained transmission objection.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Christianity was relatively small and not widespread before Constantine, in part because it had not yet been legalized.

orphanFallback.rationale: As a constructive qualification, the concession narrows the continuity claim to institutional and doctrinal persistence rather than unsupported pre-Constantinian numerical prevalence.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: A hierarchy of church leaders attested in the first-century New Testament persisted through the pre-Nicene period despite internal conflict, supporting identification of a continuous Catholic institution.

orphanFallback.rationale: The excerpt directly advances hierarchy and persistence from the first century to Nicaea as affirmative evidence for institutional continuity, requiring no earlier opposing move.

chunk-002:c002-04.proposition: Syriac and Roman churches substantially agree in Christology, Trinitarian theology, and Marian belief despite differences in terminology.

orphanFallback.rationale: The specified areas of doctrinal agreement provide a self-contained constructive example of regional convergence within ancient apostolic Christianity.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac churches retain common essential doctrines and councils, making their divisions narrower than their differences from evangelical Protestantism.

orphanFallback.rationale: The shared councils and essential doctrines cited in the excerpt affirmatively support continuity among apostolic communions without depending on any preceding objection.
